problem: Semantic cues for ObjectGoal navigation (e.g., 'bedrooms are down the hallway') are usually learned end-to-end with RL. That needs millions of simulator interactions with dense, instrumented rewards and generalizes poorly. Learning these cues instead from passive Internet video is hard for three reasons: the videos have no action labels, no goal or intent labels, and the behavior shown is not optimal. This breaks standard imitation learning and IRL assumptions.
motivation: Semantic navigation priors are just spatial co-occurrence statistics of visual patterns, and YouTube real-estate tours contain many such examples at essentially zero cost. They also span far more (and more diverse) homes than 3D scans. The paper argues that off-policy Q-learning can recover optimal goal-reaching values from non-optimal, action-free videos once they are pseudo-labeled, which avoids the sample complexity of RL.
key_idea: Pseudo-label YouTube house-tour frame pairs with robot actions (from an inverse model trained on 40K random interactions) and with object-presence rewards (from Mask R-CNN), then run off-policy Double-DQN Q-learning to get per-category image value functions f(I,c)=max_a Q(I,a,c). These values drive a hierarchical topological-graph explorer to find objects in unseen environments.
insight: Q-learning over pseudo-labeled actions recovers the optimal value function from sub-optimal video, which action-agnostic policy evaluation cannot. In a branching toy environment where videos mostly show sub-optimal paths, Q-learning reaches the near goal with SPL 0.88 versus 0.34 for TD(0) policy evaluation. The pipeline is robust to its noisy pseudo-labels: on Etrain, swapping in true actions, true detections or true reward locations barely changes OS-SPL (0.40 → 0.41/0.40/0.41), and optimal trajectories only give 0.43. Two changes help clearly: adding the detector score to goal sampling (0.46), since the detector gives a peaky near-range signal while f(I,c) helps at long range, and training on 360° video (0.47), which avoids perceptual aliasing when Q-values propagate through wall-facing views. Behavior cloning on the same data needs the video and robot action spaces to match (OS-SPL 0.25 on YouTube vs 0.34–0.36 on synthetic). VLV uses actions only indirectly and is more tolerant of this mismatch.
method: Action grounding (inverse model): a ResNet-18 encodes I_t and I_{t+1}; the stacked features pass through 2 conv + 2 FC layers to predict the intervening action (fwd 25cm / left 30° / right 30°). It is trained with cross-entropy on 40K random-action frames from Etrain Gibson scenes (~96% held-out accuracy) and used to pseudo-label every video transition.

Goal labeling: a COCO-trained Mask R-CNN runs on each video frame. Frames whose detection scores for a category fall in the top 10% get reward +1 for that category (bed, chair, couch, dining table, toilet), otherwise 0.

Off-policy Q-learning: Double DQN on (I_t, â_t, I_{t+1}, r^c_{t+1}) quadruples from 550K YouTube transitions (1 frame / 1.5 s), with γ=0.99 and target clipped to [0,1]. The Q-network is an ImageNet ResNet-18 trunk + 3×3×64 conv + FC[512,256,15] reshaped to 3 actions × 5 classes, trained with Adam lr 1e-4 for 300K batches of 16 (22 h, 1 GPU). The value is f(I,c)=max_a Q(I,a,c).

High-level policy: a topological graph whose nodes store 12 views (rotating 12×30°). Each view is scored by f_comb = λ1 f(I,c) + λ2·1[D≥0.5](1+D_coco(I,c)) + 0.05λ3·max(10−d,0), with λ=1. The highest-scoring direction is popped from a priority heap, and k=100 short-term goals are sampled 1–2 m from the node within ±7°.

Low-level policy: a depth-based occupancy map plus Fast Marching Method planner (adapted from Gupta's map-plan baseline) drives FORWARD/LEFT/RIGHT actions. It returns control on success, on infeasibility, or on timeout.

Stopping rule (Policy Stop): stop when a Mask R-CNN detection of class c has confidence ≥0.75 and the median depth inside its mask is ≤ d_c. d_c is a per-category threshold tuned on 100 Etrain episodes. The same rule is applied to all baselines because it beat their own stop actions.

setting.backbone: ResNet-18 (ImageNet-init) Q-network trained with Double DQN on pseudo-labeled videos; ResNet-18 inverse model; frozen COCO Mask R-CNN detector; classical occupancy-map + FMM low-level planner
setting.training_data: YouTube House Tours dataset: 1387 real-estate tour videos, 119 h, sampled every 1.5 s → 550K transition tuples (outdoor/people frames removed). Plus 40K reward-free random-action interaction frames in the Etrain Gibson scenes for the inverse model. Mask R-CNN pretrained on MS-COCO. Variants: synthetic videos V_syn from 85 Gibson Evideo scenes (300 trajectories/scene, avg 40 steps, 4-view panoramas); strong-supervision variant uses GT Q-values from semantically labeled Evideo meshes.
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (90° FoV, camera at 1.25 m) + perfect pose; 12-view 360° panoramas gathered by rotating at each semantic-reasoning node
setting.action_space: low-level FORWARD 0.25 m / TURN 30° / STOP, driven by high-level short-term goals 1–2 m away
setting.privileged: perfect agent localization/pose assumed; Oracle Stop setting auto-terminates the episode as success within 1 m of the target (OS-* metrics); stop-distance thresholds tuned on Etrain episodes

numbers.extra: Custom ObjectGoal set, not the SemExp Gibson ObjectNav episodes: 1075 episodes on the 5 Gibson tiny-val scenes, 5 classes (bed, chair, couch, dining table, toilet), success ≤1 m. Perfect pose; 40K reward-free interaction frames in Etrain + 550K YouTube transitions. SPL/SR = Policy Stop (hand-crafted Mask R-CNN+depth stop rule); OS-SPL/OS-SR = Oracle Stop; 90% bootstrap CI ±0.02–0.03.

numbers_note: Evaluation uses the paper's own ObjectGoal episodes: 1075 episodes on the 5 Gibson tiny-val scenes (Collierville, Corozal, Darden, Markleeville, Wiconisco), 5 categories, 1 m success radius, perfect pose. This is not the SemExp/Habitat Gibson ObjectNav episode set, so the numbers are not directly comparable to it. Metrics are printed as fractions with 90% bootstrap CIs and converted here to 0–100. SPL/SR map to Policy Stop; OS-SPL/OS-SR are Oracle Stop (the paper's own naming). Per-difficulty (easy/medium/hard) and per-class breakdowns are in Tables S2–S5. Ablations in Table S6 were evaluated on the training scenes Etrain and are not listed. Minor internal inconsistencies: the text says the best RL model is compared to '0.50 and 75% for our method' while Table 1 gives 0.53/0.79. The text also says BC on V̂syn gets 0.36 OS-SPL, while Table S2 reports 0.34 overall. Policy Stop SR for VLV (V̂yt) is ±0.03 in Table 1 but ±0.02 in Table S4.
results: With only 40K reward-free interaction frames plus YouTube videos, VLV reaches Oracle-Stop SPL/SR of 0.53/0.79 and Policy-Stop SPL/SR of 0.22/0.39 on unseen Gibson scenes. This beats the Detection Seeker exploration baseline (0.46/0.75; 0.19/0.37) and the best end-to-end PPO RL (0.29/0.56 OS, using 250× more interaction, 6× more environments and dense rewards). It also beats behavior cloning on the same pseudo-labeled videos (0.25/0.53). VLV nearly matches a value function strongly supervised from labeled 3D maps (0.55 OS-SPL), and combining the two gives 0.57 OS-SPL.
limitations: Assumes perfect agent localization and depth-based mapping; evaluated only in simulation on 5 Gibson scenes and 5 object classes, with a custom episode set and no real-robot test.

The learned value is optimal under the video-recording agent's dynamics, which may differ from the robot's action space at fine time scales. YouTube videos lack 360° context, which causes perceptual aliasing (360° training data improved OS-SPL 0.40→0.47 in ablation).

Absolute Policy-Stop performance is low (SPL 0.22) and relies on a hand-crafted Mask R-CNN + depth stop rule with per-category tuned thresholds. Gathering 12-view panoramas at every reasoning node also costs 12 steps.
